At printed p.110 (pdf page 10), text-layer lines 452-454 and a fresh extracted text of page 10 both read exactly: '4.4 STRESS / The penultimate syllable is stressed. Stress moves to the right with the addition of suffixes to a root.' That is the entire subsection; 4.5 VARIATION follows immediately. I read the whole phonology chapter (sec. 4, pp.106-111: 4.1 consonants, 4.2 vowels incl. a long/short contrast for i e a o u, 4.3 phonotactics, 4.4 stress, 4.5 variation, 4.6 orthography): nothing qualifies the stress rule -- no weight condition tied to th…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; when suffixes are added the stress shifts rightward so that it remains penultimate in the suffixed word (i.e. the domain is the whole inflected word, not the root).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. (Footnote 2, p.101, notes the personal name Rantes [rantres] breaks a phonotactic generalisation, not a stress one.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root plus suffixes); statement based on elicited citation forms from a single last fluent speaker (Aiar Rantes), data gathered 1988 and 1990; author calls it a salvage sketch, not an in-depth study.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Nāti (Crowley's spelling; speakers' own name Nati; Charpentier's 'Nahati') of Wintua/Windua village, Southwest Bay, Malakula = Glottolog nati1244 exactly; no ISO 639-3 code. Data from one of the last speakers (Aiar Rantes), so the description is effectively an idiolect of a moribund language; Crowley notes some possible intrusion from the speaker's other languages (sec. 4.5).
